input: Consider, by way of a worked example, a flat wall constructed from firebrick, having a thickness of 20 mm, which serves to separate two process streams that are at different temperatures. The thermal conductivity that characterises the wall material is 1.1 W m-1 K-1, and measurements indicate that the temperature difference maintained across the wall amounts to 127 K. If the conduction process is treated as steady in character and as taking place in one dimension only, the corresponding heat flux through the wall can be evaluated, and the value that emerges from the evaluation is 6985 W m-2 under the stated conditions. One point that deserves to be emphasised in connection with this result is that surface (film) resistances have been left out of the estimate altogether, and were those resistances to be brought into the picture, the consequence would be a heat flux lower than the one reported here, so the figure should be read as relating purely to the wall itself. The example also takes the temperature difference as the difference between the two faces of the brick, which is the difference the wall actually experiences, and not as the difference between the bulk temperatures of the two streams, which would be larger once the films are taken into account. It should be understood that the purpose of an example of this kind is to isolate the behaviour of the wall itself, and it achieves that purpose precisely by leaving to one side the complications that attend the transfer of heat from a stream to a surface and from the surface into the stream on the far side, complications that would need to be addressed in full in any calculation that was intended to predict the performance of an actual installation rather than to exhibit the conduction step in isolation.
target: Steady one-dimensional conduction through a flat firebrick wall gives a heat flux of 6985 W m-2 at the stated conditions. The wall thickness is 20 mm, the thermal conductivity $k$ of the firebrick is 1.1 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 127 K. The flux follows from the conductivity and the temperature difference divided by the thickness: the thickness is the length the heat crosses, and it sets the scale of the result together with the difference driving it. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux. The reported figure is thus the conduction flux within the brick, stated without the two surface resistances that a complete wall calculation places in series with it. The series arrangement fixes the direction of the correction without fixing its size. The same flux passes through film, brick, and film in turn, the total temperature difference divides among them in proportion to their resistances, and the share falling across the brick is smaller than the whole. How much smaller depends on film coefficients this example does not state, so the example reports the brick alone and names what it omits. The steadiness assumption does the same kind of work as the film exclusion: it limits the claim. A wall still changing temperature stores or releases heat as it changes, the flux entering one face differs from the flux leaving the other, and no single flux describes the wall. The stated value belongs to the settled state, in which the temperature profile through the brick is fixed and the flux is the same at every plane within it. The profile in that state is a straight line between the face temperatures, because the conductivity is taken as constant and no heat is generated within the wall, and the flux can be read from the steepness of that line as directly as from the stated formula.
